hazards.accept-warm-load: You waved the truck off without reading the reefer display. A trailer that has been running warm on the road has already started this delivery behind, and produce that spent the trip too warm does not recover once it is inside a cold walk-in.
hazards.ethylene-mix: That banana case is stacked flush against the leafy greens. Bananas are one of the produce department's own heaviest ethylene producers, and stacking one against an ethylene-sensitive case starts ripening — and yellowing — the case next to it before it ever reaches the floor.
hazards.prop-cooler-door: You propped the walk-in door open with the pallet instead of closing it behind you. A propped cooler door is a slow, continuous temperature excursion for every case already inside it, not just the one you are wheeling through.
hazards.wet-dock-crossing: You drove the loaded jack straight across the wet, icy patch on the apron instead of matting or clearing it first. A dock apron gets wet from every reefer that runs and every case that drips, and OSHA's walking-working-surfaces rule exists because that surface takes a loaded pallet jack down as easily as it takes a person.

interrupts.alert: The driver has climbed back into the cab and is revving the engine — two more stops on the route, and the chocks haven't even been checked yet.
interrupts.cue: This trailer does not get treated as parked until the chocks are actually confirmed.
interrupts.missNote: You let the driver's hurry carry the moment and never confirmed the chocks. If that trailer had crept even a few inches with a hand truck on the plate, the schedule that pressured you would not have been the thing anyone remembered.
interrupts.why: A driver's schedule is not a reason to skip the one check that keeps this trailer from creeping while somebody is standing on the dock plate — confirm the chocks before anything else about the driver's hurry matters.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the wheel chocks — confirm them before the driver's schedule decides anything else about this delivery.

interrupts.alert: A stock clerk has grabbed the culled berry flat off the reject zone by mistake and is wheeling it toward the walk-in with the rest of the order.
interrupts.cue: Stop that case before it reaches the walk-in — it already failed inspection.
interrupts.missNote: The culled case went into the walk-in with everything else. It now reads, to every clerk who opens that door, exactly like every other case on the shelf — the refusal log sitting back on the dock is the only thing that ever said otherwise.
interrupts.why: A culled case that reaches the walk-in stops being a cull and starts being inventory — the next clerk who opens that door has no way to know it already failed. Catching it here, on the dock, is the last easy chance.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the reject zone — redirect that case back to it before the clerk reaches the walk-in door.

lateNotes.damaged-case: The reject zone is where this case goes the moment you decide it fails — not back on the pallet, not into the walk-in.
lateNotes.pallet-jack: The walk-in is the last stop, not a stop along the way — nothing gets set down between the dock and the cooler door once it has passed inspection.

name: Produce Receiving, Cold Chain & Pallet Jack

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Compare the delivery invoice to today's produce order before the truck is unloaded.
steps.prompt: Compare the delivery invoice to today's produce order before the truck is unloaded.
steps.title: Check the invoice against the order
steps.why: The invoice is the only record of what was supposed to arrive, at what count. Catching a shortage or a substitution here is a phone call to the supplier; catching it after the truck has left is a credit dispute nobody can prove.

steps.cue: Read the truck's own reefer temperature through the window and commit once it shows the load has held cold the whole trip.

gauge.label: REEFER BOX TEMP
gauge.missNote: Reefer is reading warm — do not break the seal on this load yet; get it re-checked before anything comes off the truck.

steps.prompt: Read the truck's own reefer temperature through the window and commit once it shows the load has held cold the whole trip.
steps.title: Read the truck's reefer display
steps.why: The reefer display is the truck's own record of the whole trip, not just the last few minutes at your dock. A trailer reading warm before the door is even open has already failed the delivery, whatever the first case you probe happens to read.

steps.cue: Open the truck doors, then bridge the gap with the dock leveler — in that order.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Wrong order — the doors open first so you can see the load, then the leveler bridges the gap you can now see.
steps.prompt: Open the truck doors, then bridge the gap with the dock leveler — in that order.
steps.title: Open the truck and bridge the dock
steps.why: The doors open onto a load that has been sealed and refrigerated for hours; the leveler only bridges a gap you can actually see once the doors are open. Dropping the leveler onto closed doors tells you nothing about the load behind them.

steps.cue: Check that both wheel chocks are seated against the trailer's tires before anyone works the dock plate.
steps.prompt: Check that both wheel chocks are seated against the trailer's tires before anyone works the dock plate.
steps.title: Confirm the trailer's wheel chocks
steps.why: A trailer with no tractor still attached can creep away from the dock under its own weight, and the gap that opens between the trailer and the leveler is exactly where a loaded pallet jack goes down. The chocks are what keep that gap from ever opening while the dock is in use.

steps.cue: Probe between two heads in the leafy greens case and commit once the reading is inside the store's posted cold range.

gauge.label: LEAFY GREENS — TEMP
gauge.missNote: Outside the posted cold range — this case is refused, not re-probed until it happens to pass.

steps.prompt: Probe between two heads in the leafy greens case and commit once the reading is inside the store's posted cold range.
steps.title: Probe the leafy greens case
steps.why: Leafy greens show field heat and cold-chain gaps faster than almost anything else on this pallet, so probing between two heads — not the outside of the case where the trailer's air has been blowing on it — is what actually tells you whether this delivery held its temperature the whole trip.

steps.cue: Two things on this pallet are not sound. Find them before anything is accepted.

decoyNotes.clean-crate: This crate is intact and dry, nothing seeping through the slats. Leave it.

itemNames.moldy-bag: a produce bag showing mold through the film

itemNotes.crushed-berries: This berry flat is crushed and leaking through the bottom of its case. Juice from one crushed flat wicks into every case stacked beneath it on the same pallet.
itemNotes.moldy-bag: Mold is visible through this bag's film. One spoiled bag left on an otherwise good pallet is what a cull is for — separating the one thing already gone from everything that is still fine.

steps.prompt: Two things on this pallet are not sound. Find them before anything is accepted.
steps.title: Walk the pallet for damage before it's accepted
steps.why: Produce is checked with your hands and your eyes on every case, not sampled on a few — a crushed flat or a spoiled bag left in place keeps doing damage to everything stacked around it for as long as it sits there.

steps.cue: Check the chart before the pallet is broken down, to see what has to be kept apart from what.
steps.prompt: Check the chart before the pallet is broken down, to see what has to be kept apart from what.
steps.title: Check the ethylene segregation chart
steps.why: Ethylene-producing produce and ethylene-sensitive produce riding the same pallet face to face is a fast way to have half a delivery ripening before it reaches the case — the chart is what tells you which is which before the segregation happens, not after a customer notices.

steps.cue: Pull the crushed berry flat and move it to the reject zone.

drag.missNote: Not in the reject zone — a culled case anywhere else on the dock is one more thing somebody has to remember not to stock.

steps.prompt: Pull the crushed berry flat and move it to the reject zone.
steps.title: Cull the failed case
steps.why: A culled case leaves the delivery physically, right away — set beside the accepted pallet, it is one distracted moment away from riding to the walk-in with everything else.

steps.cue: Write the item, the reason and the quantity culled on the refusal log.
steps.prompt: Write the item, the reason and the quantity culled on the refusal log.
steps.title: Log the cull
steps.why: The refusal log is what gets a credit from the supplier and tells the next shift why a case on the invoice never made it to the floor. Without it, a cull is just missing inventory nobody can explain.

steps.cue: Ratchet the strap down over the stacked accepted cases before the jack ever moves.
steps.prompt: Ratchet the strap down over the stacked accepted cases before the jack ever moves.
steps.title: Strap the pallet jack's load
steps.why: A stack that shifts on a moving pallet jack comes down on whoever is driving it, not on the floor first. The strap is what turns a stack of separate cases into one load that goes exactly where the jack points it.

steps.cue: Sound the horn at both blind corners and hold a steady, balanced pace the whole way to the walk-in door.

checks.note: Blind corner past the empty-pallet rack — horn before you round it.
Blind corner into the walk-in alcove — horn again before the door swings your way.

steps.holdBreakNote: Out of the lane or out of the load's speed band — settle the jack and hold a steady, balanced pace the rest of the way.
steps.prompt: Sound the horn at both blind corners and hold a steady, balanced pace the whole way to the walk-in door.
steps.title: Drive the load to the walk-in
steps.why: The backroom aisle to the walk-in runs past two blind corners a stock clerk could step around at any moment, and a pallet jack loaded to eye height cannot be stopped the way a person on foot can. The horn is what buys the half-second a corner does not give you any other way.

steps.cue: Read the walk-in cooler's posted thermometer and commit once it shows the room is inside its own range.

gauge.label: WALK-IN TEMP
gauge.missNote: The walk-in itself is reading outside its posted range — flag it before this pallet goes inside, not after.

steps.prompt: Read the walk-in cooler's posted thermometer and commit once it shows the room is inside its own range.
steps.title: Read the walk-in's own thermometer
steps.why: The delivery's cold chain is not actually unbroken until the room it lands in is proven cold too — a probe that passed at the dock means nothing if the pallet is about to sit inside a walk-in that has been running warm all shift.

steps.cue: Check the FIFO card and place the new pallet behind whatever produce is already in the walk-in.
steps.prompt: Check the FIFO card and place the new pallet behind whatever produce is already in the walk-in.
steps.title: Rotate the stock by date
steps.why: First in, first out only works if the newest pallet actually goes behind the oldest one every single time — put it in front because it's closer to the door, and the case in back is what a clerk finds spoiled next week.

steps.cue: Sign the receiving log to close out the delivery.
steps.prompt: Sign the receiving log to close out the delivery.
steps.title: Sign the receiving log
steps.why: The signature is the clerk taking responsibility for every reading on this delivery — what was accepted, what was culled and why, and what the walk-in itself read when the pallet went inside.

tagline: A produce delivery checked, culled and segregated at the dock, then driven on the pallet jack to the walk-in without ever breaking the cold chain
